2.text: I heard of no cases of cannibalism among the Chukchee, notwithstanding

3.text: the fact that several cases of famine which wiped out whole villages were still

4.text: fresh in the memory of the people. On the other hand, a Yukaghir family

5.text: which was starved in 1895 on the Middle Omolon had recourse to the most

6.text: horrible cannibalism. Nor am I aware of any cases of exposure of new-born

7.text: girls, as among the American Eskimo. New-born babes, indeed, after the death

8.text: of their mothers, are frequently smothered, and carried out with them to the

9.text: funeral-places, but this is because of the impossibility of raising them. I have

10.text: heard, too, of women just delivered, who, when feeling very ill, would smother

11.text: their children as a sacrifice to the spirits.

12.text: Hospitality to travellers is much more liberal among the Maritime Chuk-

13.text: chee than among the reindeer-breeders. The Arctic people say, that, even

14.text: if a guest wants to strike his host, the latter must continue to be friendly.

15.text: During my last journey along the Pacific coast, when we were several times

16.text: detained in Chukchee or Eskimo dwellings by a storm, it would often happen

17.text: that the master of the house, having little blubber and no wood to feed the

18.text: fire, would break up his sleds, and even tear out one by one the wooden

19.text: supports of his house, thus endangering its safety.

20.text: With the Reindeer people it is otherwise. First of all, they are much

21.text: more superstitious about the “shunning” of diseases. In times of disease, even
21.note: Curly quotes per keying_spec.md §1/§5.6; machine text had opening “ but a straight closing " for the same pair.

22.text: a healthy traveller, when he comes to a Chukchee camp from afar, especially

23.text: if he arrives at night, runs the risk of not being admitted to any of the tents.

24.text: This would never happen in a Maritime village. Many travellers of the

25.text: Reindeer tribe are themselves averse to entering strange houses at such times,

26.text: and prefer to sleep in the open, content with an incantation against the spirits,

27.text: in lieu of supper. Even at ordinary times a guest arriving at the camp is

28.text: considered as having no more rights than the inmates of the house. He will

29.text: have to wait outside with the other people till evening, when the sleeping-

30.text: room is made ready. Sometimes he will be given no food until the time of

31.text: the principal meal, which is eaten in the evening. At the time of the great

32.text: reindeer races, scores of people come to take part in the races or to look on.
32.note: Zoomed at 2x: the mark over the a in "take" is a stray ink speck, not a diacritic — ordinary English word, plain a.

33.text: Often they are given no food at all, and, after a whole day spent in the open,

34.text: return in the evening to their respective camps, scattered around at a distance

35.text: of some thirty or forty miles.

36.text: Theft among the Maritime Chukchee is comparatively rare. To steal

37.text: from a neighbor in the same village is considered very improper. It is cus-

38.text: tomary for a stranger to place all his property in the storehouse of his host

39.text: and under his personal care. In recent years, however, the increase of trade
39.note: Zoomed at 2x: machine text read "vears"; printed word is "years".

40.text: has spoiled this native honesty. Now, in all large villages, the owners of wooden

41.text: storehouses, which are bought from the whalers, carefully lock their doors with

42.text: steel padlocks for fear of robbers. During my stay in Indian Point a shaman
